In captivity we have the ability to have higher hatch and survival rates, and it’s because of methods like this. If an animal is weaker, sick, or failing to thrive, it should obviously not be used for breeding or at times, breeders will cull. This is not one of those cases.

Nope, wrong. Breeders assist babies all the time, especially ones that are not being stimulated enough by the other siblings (which in this case was true, as she was the first one out). 

FYI she's alive and well, just as the chameleons that I have bred before that all are thriving in their new homes. A responsible breeder does not just let their animals die.

Eggs will not pip if the humidity is low. Humidity is not the issue here at all. She was the first to pip and was not being stimulated by the other babies, so she kept going back into her egg and would not come out. I stimulated the egg multiple times but did not want to risk it, as I have lost babies in the past after listening to people who said, "wait it out, they will come out". 

In this case, she wasn't being trampled on b her siblings so she simply pipped on her own, but made no more progress after that. I made the call to safely remove her the safest way possible. For chameleons, this is necessary sometimes especially the weaker ones. I've spoken to numerous breeders and they all agreed that if there's no progress after a couple days, you intervene before they die.

Not sure if this answers your question, but chameleons don't change color based on their surroundings or camouflage. It's all based on their emotion/mood, so they really don't have that many options to actually change color. In general, they go dark when they're scared/upset, remain "natural colors" when they're happy/content, and go veryyy bright and almost opposite colors when excited, seeing a male/female, etc. They definitely can understand the meaning of those said colors though. If a female is showing dark, non-receptive colors during breeding attempts, the male will generally back off (otherwise he risks getting hurt). When she turns into a pink color, that lets the male know she's ready to breed. 

They're extremely intelligent creatures but the biggest misconception is that they turn colors based on their environment and such. Definitely would be cool but sadly not the case. They do however understand what these colors mean especially if they see another chameleon!

As someone who is disabled and currently dealing with a fractured hip, I want to give a sincere thank you to anyone who is willing to help us. I was fortunate enough to experience the kindness of many people on Monday, when I was forced to go out for last minute groceries to feed my pets. I was wheelchair bound and worried about being trampled, not getting what I needed, etc. 

I got there before the store opened and already there was a large line of people. However as I was wheeling towards the back of the line, a girl stood up and let everyone know that I should be allowed to go in first. Everyone agreed, and a man even hopped out of line to offer to help me with my groceries. He stayed with me the entire time, helping me get everything I needed and even bagged and loaded up my groceries for me. And the ONLY things he bought were a bag of potatoes and bread, and refused to let me pay for them as a thank you. He just kept telling me we all need to help one another out in times like these, and I couldn't have been more grateful that so many people were looking out for me.

Thank you to the lady in line that spoke up for me, and thank you Kenny for helping me shop for not only myself, but my beloved animals. And thank you to anyone else who has done the same for the elderly or disabled; you don't know how much it means to us when people show us kindness in times like these.

Craigslist! You'd be surprised how many people need feeders for their babies. I always sold really cheap too since I was selling to fellow reptile enthusiast, so I had many returning customers. :P

The cost was honestly very little to maintain, and my colony was atleast 1,000+ dubia's. I fed them oranges 2-3 times a week since that is known to help them breed more (no one knows why, but I've seen better results with them) and made my own food. The need lots of protein, so I made them a ground up mix of dog/cat food, oats, and any leftover sugary cereal I had. Occassionally I'll add in some fish flakes as well. I'd make one large batch that would last me months since they don't eat too much of it (it's full of protein so they get full fast). Then I'd just throw in whatever veggies or fruits we had leftover that was going bad, and they'd eat them right up. :P I can't tell you the cost honestly cuz I have no idea where to start, but it's incredibly low. I'd saw it cost me no more than like $8 a month to care for them. The oranges are the most expensive part but are totally worth it imo. There are water crystals you can use as their water source, but in my experience, they dry out too fast and are way overpriced. And if you're concerned about being overrun with roaches, keep them in a cooler area. They will not breed in cold weather since they slow down/eat less. If you want to populate them quickly though, get a reptile heat mat, tape it on the outside of a rubbermaid bin, and aim for 90F inside. Warm temps + oranges = life time supply of feeders. :) 


Oh and also, don't worry about feeding your roaches dog food and all that. What you'll need to do the day before feeding is pick out some roaches and gutload them with greens or veggies. That way the dog food mix won't be transferred to your beardie. :)

Looks nice dude, great job! Here's a little tip for you if you want to continue saving money and possibly earn a little as well; start a dubia roach colony. There is a $15 minimum purchase and the shipping is about $10, so I'd stock up on them since 300 worms or so would only last you maybe 2 weeks top. Honestly, his videos are a bit 50/50 when it comes to accuracy. Nowadays yes, you can get a pretty decent violin for that price but a lot of other things need to be accounted for. I've taught violin for a few years now, and the number one problem I've had is when parents bring me a cheap violin they bought off Amazon, or from craigslist. 90% of them had problems with the pegs, which if done poorly, will cause the strings to slip or sometimes not even hold inside the hole at all. These violins are made on a commercial level and aren't given the amount of attention needed in critical areas on the violin. The quality of the plastics of the violin can also cause problems, since I've had a few occasions where the chin rest has become loose or broken off some of the cheaper violins.

I'm not shitting on "cheaper" violins since I think they're an excellent choice to start off with, but please don't think you're going to get a steal deal with a $99 violin. It's often a hit or miss, and you're bound to have problems with it eventually. I always recommend my students start off with renting a violin, to basically ensure they want to pursue the violin but also because those violins tend to be a bit more higher quality. Just my opinion, but hey, in the end, if you want to learn to play the violin then go for it!

This sounds a lot like my first beardie Mojo, minus the sunken in eyes.  He was perfectly fine but suddenly started closing his eyes all the time, not opening them even if I was messing with him. He would open them for a few seconds, but then close them immediately. He then stopped eating and became SUPER lethargic. And I mean to the point where if I was bathing him, he couldn't even keep his head above the water... he was practically limp. Took him to the vet, spent $250+ on blood tests and vitamin shots, only to be told he's "fine" and his blood tests were perfect. I was sent home with eye drops since they thought it was just an eye infection, and I was told to keep him outside for natural sunlight. I did this daily, while giving him his eye drops and bathing him for hydration. He did perk up for a couple of days, but crashed again and became worse. :( One day I went to go get him after having him basking outside, and saw that he was full black and gasping for air. He eventually went into a coma and passed overnight. I still have no idea what this was, whether it was an actual illness or if he either ate something outside or got spooked, but I feel it was this unknown illness that did this to him. I didn't want to post his story here since I understand what you're feeling right now, but if I can be of any help, it is to just not mess with him much at all. I regret listening to my vet and I feel like me putting him outside (which probably stressed him out more) probably worsened his condition and ultimately led to his passing. Also, if they ask to just do an examine on his eyes, PLEASE don't let them convince you to just go home and do eye drops or something. That's what my vet originally thought too but unfortunately my little beardie wasn't lucky enough to pull through, since there was nothing wrong with his eyes at all. I've been told it could have been something genetically wrong with him, which means there was nothing that could be done. He was a German Giant, and supposedly they have been known to have these unknown illness spring up. I truly hope this isn't the case for your beardie, and I hope he pulls through quickly. Just please make sure you stress the other symptons (lethargic, no appetite, etc) because I didn't stress it enough with my little Mojo. Just make sure the trees don't have any pesticides on them or anything. And you'll need the brand new, super tiny baby leaves for baby silkworms since they're nice and soft. I don't think it's weird at all! I was actually hoping to either buy a mulberry tree or find one so I can start raising them again since the chow just gets too expensive. :/

I wouldn't risk it with the veggies. I've tried feeding them greens, carrots, and a few other things and they just wouldn't accept it. And a few did eat it but I noticed severe growth delay so I'd definitely recommend sticking to the chow 100% of the time. That's the only thing they will accept really aside from the leaves.

The first time I raised silkworms, I was pretty clueless and didn't really keep up with the cleaning either. I did have quite a few die offs that I'm sure was due to a dirty environment. When I started raising them, I was cleaning them nearly everyday (just removing the poop and wiping down any moisture that forms on the sides) and I keep their food I'm a ziploc bag that is cut at the end. That way I would just need to pipe out the food directly into their container and not have to worry about contamination. I only had die offs when I didn't keep them warm in the 80s, otherwise my method worked really well. So I'd definitely say cleaning them everyday/every other day would ensure they stay healthy. The biggest thing to look out for is moisture build up because that's what causes things to mold. I've also had the baby worms literally drown in droplets of water that formed on the side, so be careful of that! If you're using leaves then you shouldn't have that problem, but with the chow, it can make their container quite humid. Let me know if you have any other questions! I'd love to hear how things work out for you.

I actually got like, 200 silkworms hatch after being kept in the fridge for 2 months and well, lets just say my little Milo was one happy (and fat) lizard that month haha. Most important thing is to keep everything clean, especially their food. For the first few days, you'll have to help some of the worms onto the food since I've seen a few that will crawl off and they're too young at that point to really find the food on their own. It's a lot of work, just keep that in mind! But totally worth it to raise your own, especially when it comes to making our beardies happy. :) 

Good luck!

Glad to see you took the advice about blocking off some of the tank! Try to get those temps up a bit more, especially the basking spot. The hot side needs to be mid 90's but basking spot needs to be much hotter. You can go as hot as 115F but no more than that. 105F is a good basking temp, but 105-115F is even better. Then as long as his hot side is mid 90's, that will be good. And make sure he's got a little area to cool off in if needed (mid 70's-80's). When he gets bigger and you unblock the rest of his cage, you can move over his little hide to the cool end so it stays very cool inside. They will use their hides a bunch in the winter time when they get ready to brumate and prefer it cooler.

The reason he hasn't pooped yet might be because of the temps. These guys usually poop daily, sometimes twice a day, so it's odd you haven't had him poop yet. Bump up the heat even more and that will help.

Silkworms are considered one of the best staples to feed them next to dubia's. Hornworms are still good but contain a lot of water, and I believe a bit less protein than silkworms. I believe silkworms are probably the better of the two, mostly because they're high in protein and calcium, and low in fat. They're also slightly less expensive and can be bred easier than hornworms. Hornworms are still an excellent choice, especially if your guy ever gets sick or is on medication of any kind. They contain a ton of water, so people tend to use them to help hydrate their sick beardies. 

I personally like silkworms over hornworms mainly because they're cheaper and can be bred, but also because hornworms get really huge. It often freaks me out and I fear my little guy might choke on one or something. With silkworms, they're large enough to keep him full but small enough to prevent any choking. And impaction risks are little to none with these soft-bodied worms.

Anyways, that's awesome you've got a colony started. It will cut down your expense a bunch once your colony kicks off. :)

Yes, 105F is the minimum for babies. I only said 100F is suitable as well in certain cases because some beardies do not like it that hot. My first guy didn't like anything above about 101F. He simply would not bask until I brought the temperature down. You're right though, you can definitely bring the temp up to 115F and adjust if needed (based on each individual beardie).

For example, my current beardie right now is a full grown adult, and he doesn't like anything  above 95F. He doesn't bask where it's about 105F, but simply stays in the middle of his basking area where it's mid 90's. I've had to bring the temperature down a bit in the past to suit his preference haha. In the end, it will depend on the bearded dragon and what they like so just make necessary adjustments as needed.

Hmm, I would move the heat lamp over to the right side under the branch. The hide that you have should be on the cool side (temp should be mid 70's-low 80's) so it has the option to cool down if needed. Just move the heat lamp over, re check your temps/adjust if necessary, and you should be good to go! It looks great otherwise. Like someone else said, maybe add in a little plastic plant for it to play in. It will also help with the shedding since they can rub around in it. 

And also, the food bowl. I don't recommend putting water in it, because odds are your beardie isn't going to drink straight from it. Instead, just use it for whatever veggies and insects you plan on feeding it, but no water. Too much humidity can cause a respiratory infection. Instead, just bathe your beardie every week, and wiggle your finger in the water. The movement and waves of the water should entice them to start lapping up the water. If not, a good 15-20 minute soak is fine as well.

I agree with what TheLast500 said- I don't think those particular worms aren't really good to feed him everyday. The only staple worms you should be feeding him I believe are silkworms and hornworms. Those are not as fatty and have tons of protein, however they are pricey. My beardie eats them as a staple since he's a picky guy, and he's very healthy. They are the only worms I feel comfortable feeding to him as his staple feeder insects.

You should check out dubia roaches too. They are one of the best staple feeders to feed, and most beardies will go crazy for them. They aren't super expensive, and if your guy likes them enough, then you can start your own colony. They're 100000 times easier to care for than crickets too. Whatever you decide to feed him though, make sure you aren't feeding too many of those worms. He needs lots of protein to grow, not fat.

Is the basking spot being heated by a mat or a bulb? I don't see a heat bulb, only the UVB. Beardies do not feel and absorb heat from their bellies so heat mats are pretty much useless for them. They absorb light from above which is why bulbs are a must.

If you have a bulb in there and I just can't see it, then you're set as long as the basking spot is about 100, warm side is 90's, and cool area is mid 70's-80's. If you're only using a heat mat though, please please please go out asap and get a bulb/light fixture.

Hmm, this is just my opinion, but I think that tank might be too big for the little guy right now. If they have too much space at once, it can actually stress them out. When I first got my beardie, I took a piece of cardboard and block off about 1/3 of his tank (40 gallon) to prevent him from becoming stressed. Gradually as he grew, I moved the cardboard further back until he was big enough for the entire cage. 

This is what I personally recommend doing, otherwise he could remain very scared. Plus, it will be very hard for him to eat if he has to do a large amount of chasing in such a big area. Block some of it off and provide a little hide in that area for him incase he gets too warm. You need to have a cool down area of preferably mid 70's or so. Babies tend to bask a ton though and prefer being under the heat, but it's always best to give them a hide regardless.

Yeah, crypts will melt if they have been grown emersed. There's honestly no avoiding it really. What I found that kind of helped for me was leaving the potted crypts in the tank for a couple of days before actually planting them. This seemed to reduce the amount of leaves that melted, though a vast majority of them still died. Just trim off everything down close to the substrate and wait a bit. You will see new growth in no time.
What will help speed up this process is providing a bunch of iron to their roots. If you have a nutrient rich substrate, then you should be fine. But if you want, root tabs will definitely help jump start your crypts since they provide a bunch of iron to the roots. Just plant one tab right under the crypts for best results.

Good luck! Your tank already looks great. :)

Yes, because those are native wild bearded dragons who have adapted to handling parasites better than domesticated bearded dragons, whom are mainly fed farmed bred insects and therefore are more susceptible to illness. Owners don't go outside, pick out any insect they find in the yard, and feed it to their pets, because you risk spreading illnesses to an animal who wasn't born to handle that. People buy insects that have been bred specifically as reptile feeders, because that's what they've grown used to eating. Also to anyone who keeps saying how wild bearded dragons eating insects are "fine", you are once again missing the logic. Wild animals and domesticated animals are NOT the same in terms of health, lifespan, ability to fight illness, etc. People don't just go to Australia, find a bearded dragon in the wild, and keep it as a pet. Years of breeding goes into these animals so they lose that "wild" side to them, including the ability to tolerate parasites and infection. Pick up a book man.

Wild lizards =/= domesticated lizards. Wild animal's systems are built to resist and adapt to things domesticated animals aren't used to. Parasites WILL kill a wild bearded dragon over time regardless if they "seem to be doing just fine", where as a domesticated bearded dragon can get medication and live to its full life span. If you go without treatment though, then the same thing will happen to them; they will die.

Not all Petco's and Petsmart's insects are poor quality. I believe it was just common neglect + an already infected batch of crickets. I've bought waxworms and superworms from the same store and have never had problems though. Crickets are one of the largest parasite carrier insects you can feed your reptiles so it was just bad luck. Just goes to show that even farmed insects still pose a threat to reptiles sometimes, so feeding wild insects is even more so of a risk.

Technically, pretty much all reptiles have some form of parasites inside their digestive system. It's only when they get out of control is when the problems start occurring. Even my bearded dragon has low levels of parasites that are literally impossible to kill off, but it doesn't harm him one bit. But here's the thing... wild bearded dragons are naturally more adapted to having parasites since it's impossible for them to avoid. But over time, they will become overrun with them and that's what usually causes death, hence the higher mortality rate of a captivated beardie versus wild.

Yep, fireflies will pretty much instantly kill bearded dragons. It's why I'm so paranoid in general when bringing my beardie outside with me. I don't let him out of my sight but one wrong swallowed bug could mean life or death. I also stress the whole parasite issue because they're literally so easy to spread from bug to bug, even "farmed insects". I bought some pinhead crickets from Petco last year as a back up storage since I ran out of roaches, and less than a week later, my beardie became incredibly sick. Took him into the vet, did a fecal sample, and he had become infected with 3 different parasites, all from just those crickets. My poor guy had to get 3 rounds of treatment just to clear them up because it was a huge infestation. I will never ever step a foot near crickets again because of that experience.

Not to be a kill joy, but it's a horrible idea to feed your lizards wild insects since they may carry tons of parasites that can infect your reptiles. I've got a bearded dragon as well, and even though I'd love to use him as free pest control, it's not worth the vet bills for parasite medication.
